## Read in dataset to variable "toxic".
toxic <- read.csv("toxicity_data.csv")

## Create a backup of "toxic" dataset. 
toxic_copy1 <- toxic
## Quick review of target variable, "Class", shows that NonToxic is 2:1 to Toxic.
toxic %>%
  count(Class)
##      Class   n
## 1 NonToxic 115
## 2    Toxic  56

Due to the relative size of this dataset, 1204 variables, it is necessary to do some sort of feature selection first to reduce the dataset to a consumable chunk of data.

– Recursive Feature Elimination: Also called ‘RFE’, is an algorithm used to select features that accuractely predict a ‘target’ variable in prediction models. RFE utilizes a backward selection process to select features. The steps are as follows:

  1. Builds model & calculates importance of all features(except ‘target’).

  2. Rank-orders features and removes ones with least importance one-by-one based on model eval metrics(RMSE,accuracy,kappa).

  3. Repeats process until a smaller set of features is achieved.

** Model can select ALL features. ** Feature selection can also be based on model or criterion(e.g., accuracy).

## First, we need to split data into train/test sets.
sample <- sample(c(TRUE,FALSE), nrow(toxic), replace = TRUE, prob=c(0.7,0.3))
train <- toxic[sample, ]
test <- toxic[!sample, ]

## Define our recursive feature elimination
control_rfe = rfeControl(functions = rfFuncs, # random forest
                      method = "repeatedcv", # repeated cv
                      repeats = 5, # number of repeats
                      number = 10) # number of folds

set.seed(50) ## for reproducibility

# Performing RFE, this may take some time
result_rfe = rfe(x = train[,-1204], 
                 y = as.factor(unlist(train[,1204])), 
                 sizes = c(1:15),
                 rfeControl = control_rfe)


print(result_rfe)
## 
## Recursive feature selection

## Show our selected features.
predictors(result_rfe)
## [1] "SpMAD_Dt"  "ATSC7i"    "Mp"        "AATS0p"    "MATS6c"    "EE_Dt"    
## [7] "SpDiam_Dt" "SpMax_Dt"  "SpAD_Dt"
## Provide a visual version of the selected features. I have subsetted the 
## results as the before graph was very difficult to interpret.
plt1 <- ggplot(data = result_rfe, metric = "Accuracy") + xlim(0,25)
plt2 <- ggplot(data = result_rfe, metric = "Kappa") + xlim(0,25) 

grid.arrange(plt1,plt2,ncol=2,top="RFE Accuracy & Kappa Results")

As seen above, we decided to limit the features to ~15 variables. RFE, or “Recursive Feature Elimination”, selected 8 as it yields the highest accuracy from cross-validation. This should greatly improve model interpretability in the future.

– MATS6c appears to have a much wider distribution compared to non-toxic. However, median values appear to be quite similar. Although, Toxic median comes out just a shade higher! Neither show a normal distribution and have apparent tails on the high end.

– MDEC.23 shows quite a visible difference between Toxic median and Non-Toxic median! Toxic also shows a much more narrow distribution and fewer outliers.

– SpMax3_Bhm shows quite an interesting spread! The outliers are quite unusual and very far from the IQR(Interquartile Range). Outliers aside, distribution shows a very normalized shape for both classes. Toxic, however, has a lower median with what appears to be a quite large Upper Quartile.

– ZMIC1 shows a very spread out distribution for both Classes. On a positive note, Toxic shows what appears to be a very significantly different median from Non-Toxic. Toxic also presents a much larger lower quartile and significant outliers.

– WTPT.5 appears to show similar medians for both classes. Toxic shows a larger lower quartile while Non-Toxic shows a large Upper quartile. Both Classes have a very large distribution.

– AATSC2e shows both classes have a very narrow distrbution. Non-Toxic has a slightly higher median value. Toxic has a very large outlier. However, we have no way to verify this is a typo or not.

Decision Tree:

train_control <- trainControl(method = "LOOCV")

set.seed(42)
sample <- sample(c(TRUE,FALSE), nrow(final_toxic), replace = TRUE, prob=c(0.7,0.3))
train_toxic <- final_toxic[sample, ]
test_toxic <- final_toxic[!sample, ]


dim(train_toxic)
## [1] 112   9
dim(test_toxic)
## [1] 59  9
## Decision Tree using "Caret"
toxic.tree = train(Class ~ ., 
                  data=train_toxic, 
                  method="rpart", 
                  trControl = train_control)

print(toxic.tree)
## CART 
## 
## 112 samples
##   8 predictor
##   2 classes: 'NonToxic', 'Toxic' 
## 
## No pre-processing
## Resampling: Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation 
## Summary of sample sizes: 111, 111, 111, 111, 111, 111, ... 
## Resampling results across tuning parameters:
## 
##   cp          Accuracy   Kappa      
##   0.02857143  0.6785714   0.24010554
##   0.08571429  0.6160714   0.02272727
##   0.12857143  0.5535714  -0.23076923
## 
## Accuracy was used to select the optimal model using the largest value.
## The final value used for the model was cp = 0.02857143.
toxic.pred <- predict(toxic.tree, newdata = test_toxic)

cat("\nPrediction Table: ")
## 
## Prediction Table:
table(toxic.pred, test_toxic$Class)
##           
## toxic.pred NonToxic Toxic
##   NonToxic       30    15
##   Toxic           8     6
cat("\nError Rate: ")
## 
## Error Rate:
round(mean(toxic.pred != test_toxic$Class),2)
## [1] 0.39
suppressMessages(library(rattle))

fancyRpartPlot(toxic.tree$finalModel)

Random Forest:

set.seed(55)
## Set our number of variables to be randomly collected
mtries <- sqrt(ncol(train_toxic))
grid <- expand.grid(.mtry=mtries)

## Assign random forest model to variable.
toxic.tree = train(Class ~ ., 
                  data=train_toxic, 
                  method="rf", 
                  metric="Accuracy",
                  tuneGrid = grid,
                  trControl = train_control)

print(toxic.tree)
## Random Forest 
## 
## 112 samples
##   8 predictor
##   2 classes: 'NonToxic', 'Toxic' 
## 
## No pre-processing
## Resampling: Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation 
## Summary of sample sizes: 111, 111, 111, 111, 111, 111, ... 
## Resampling results:
## 
##   Accuracy   Kappa    
##   0.7053571  0.2235294
## 
## Tuning parameter 'mtry' was held constant at a value of 3
toxic.pred <- predict(toxic.tree, newdata = test_toxic)

cat("\nPrediction Table: ")
## 
## Prediction Table:
table(toxic.pred, test_toxic$Class)
##           
## toxic.pred NonToxic Toxic
##   NonToxic       31    12
##   Toxic           7     9
cat("\nError Rate: ")
## 
## Error Rate:
round(mean(toxic.pred != test_toxic$Class),2)
## [1] 0.32

Random Forest reduces test error from 0.39 to 0.32 — a 7-percentage-point absolute improvement over the single Decision Tree baseline.
